paper_metadata.title: Quantum advantage of Monte Carlo option pricing

summary: The paper analyzes quantum Monte Carlo option pricing using Quantum Amplitude Estimation in noisy Qiskit simulations. It shows that a Fourier-series payoff approximation outperforms the standard rescaling method and estimates that quantum advantage over classical Monte Carlo would require ≈20 logical qubits and two‑qubit gate error rates below about 10^-6, far beyond current hardware (~10^-2–10^-3).

experiments.description: Quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo option pricing for European call options using quantum amplitude estimation, comparing rescaling and Fourier-series function approximation under depolarizing noise in Qiskit simulations.

algorithm.variant: Quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo (QAMC) with standard QAE; compared rescaling technique and Fourier-series-based function application

hyperparameters.Grover_schedule: exponentially increasing schedule with base 2: m0=0, mk=2^(k-1) for k>0
hyperparameters.truncation_parameter_w: varied from 0.5 to 10 (30 evenly spaced values)
hyperparameters.rescaling_parameter_c: varied from 1e-5 to 100 (30 logarithmically spaced values)
hyperparameters.noise_ratio: two-qubit error to one-qubit error ratio e2/e1=30

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Not reported; optimization performed by grid search over n, w, c, lmax, and schedule length

optimizer_settings.step_size: n step 1; w 30 evenly spaced; c 30 log-spaced; lmax step 1

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Log-normal asset-price distribution discretized into 2^n bins and loaded into n state-preparation qubits; comparator uses n ancilla qubits; payoff encoded on one payoff qubit
problem_formulation.objective_function: Price of a European call option: discounted expectation E[e^{-rT} max(S_T-K,0)] under Black-Scholes-Merton log-normal distribution
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Truncation of distribution to [E(S_T)-w*Var(S_T), E(S_T)+w*Var(S_T)] and discretization into 2^n bins; payoff approximated either by rescaling or Fourier-series function approximation
problem_formulation.num_ancilla_qubits: n ancilla qubits for comparator circuit, plus one payoff qubit

problem_instance.description: European call option pricing under the Black-Scholes-Merton model

dataset_specification.description: At-the-money options with S0=K=2, T=1; parameter grid over r and nu

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Analytic log-normal distribution truncated and discretized; no empirical dataset used
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Noisy Qiskit simulations; optimization over parameter grid; comparison of quantum and classical pricing errors; 1000 repeated maximum-likelihood simulations for a simple 2-qubit case to estimate finite-sample standard deviation

quantum_resources.qubit_type: simulated physical qubits (no error correction; depolarizing noise model)

hardware.provider: IBM Qiskit simulator environment (no physical device used)

implementation_details.transpilation_target: IBM basis gates {CX, X, SX, RZ}
implementation_details.classical_solver: Classical Monte Carlo / Black-Scholes analytic benchmark
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Grid search over algorithm parameters; analytic truncation and variance formulas
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Maximum-likelihood estimation for QAE probabilities; error aggregation from statistical and systematic components

speedup_claims.conditions: ideal quantum amplitude estimation; ignoring noise and systematic errors
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper emphasizes that systematic errors and hardware noise can prevent practical advantage; the quadratic speedup is the standard QAE claim.

speedup_claims.factor: quantum advantage for most tested options only when CX error rate is around 1e-6 to 1e-7
speedup_claims.conditions: noisy Qiskit simulations of European call option pricing with optimized parameters
speedup_claims.caveats: Advantage is highly variable due to systematic errors; Fourier function approximation outperforms rescaling across the tested grid.

speedup_claims.conditions: under sufficiently low noise / fault-tolerant-like conditions
speedup_claims.caveats: This is an extrapolated estimate, not directly simulated at full scale.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(1/N) estimation error for QAE; quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo sampling
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(1/sqrt(N)) estimation error for classical Monte Carlo sampling
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: Paper reports quantum advantage for most options only when CX error rate is around 1e-6 to 1e-7; about 20 logical qubits may suffice

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Estimated advantage requires CX error rates ≈10^-6–10^-7 and ~20 logical qubits; current devices have ~10^-2–10^-3 error rates
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: ≈20 logical qubits with two‑qubit gate error ≤10^-6; likely requiring full fault‑tolerant error correction
limiting_factors: Two‑qubit gate error must drop from ~10^-2–10^-3 to ≤10^-6
State preparation circuit scales exponentially with qubit count
Systematic errors from discretization, truncation, and payoff approximation
Amplitude estimation circuits accumulate noise through repeated Grover iterations

notes: num_qubits inferred from stated formula 2n+1 and reported simulation limit n=13; the paper explicitly states total qubits necessary is 2n+1 and discusses simulations up to 13 qubits due to computational cost.
circuit_depth not explicitly reported; left null.
The paper uses Qiskit noisy simulation with depolarizing channels and no named QPU, so hardware.type is simulator_noisy.
Classical Monte Carlo and Black-Scholes are baselines, not separate experiments.
Authors explicitly conclude that quantum advantage would require CX error rates around 10^-6.
All results are from noisy classical simulation; no QPU experiments are performed.
